    What is the spring equinox?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    In 2026, the spring (vernal) equinox in the Northern Hemisphere occurs on
    Friday, March 20, at 14:46 UTC (10:46 a.m. EDT), marking the official start of astronomical spring. It is the moment the sun crosses directly over the Earth’s equator, resulting in nearly equal amounts of daylight and darkness worldwide. 
    Key Facts About the Spring Equinox 
    • Definition: The term comes from Latin, meaning "equal night" (aequus and nox), signaling a balance between day and night.
    • When does spring start: While meteorological spring starts March 1, the astronomical spring begins at this precise equinox moment, usually on March 20 or 21.

      Cultural Celebrations. How is the spring equinox celebrated in different cultures?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Spring equinox celebrations worldwide focus on themes of renewal, fertility, and balance, featuring unique traditions like India's vibrant Holi color festival, Japan's ancestor-honoring Shunbun no Hi, Iran's ancient Persian New Year Nowruz with its Haft-Seen table, Mexico's Mayan serpent shadow at Chichen Itza, and Pagan Ostara rituals involving eggs and new growth, reflecting a universal greeting to spring.
       
      Ancient & Indigenous Traditions
      • Mexico (Chichen Itza): The famous "Serpent of Light" illusion appears as a shadow serpent descends the Temple of Kukulkan, connecting to the feathered serpent deity. 
      • Mayan (Teotihuacan): Thousands gather to climb the Pyramid of the Sun, wearing white to absorb solar energy. 
      • Stonehenge (UK): Ancient Celts and modern Druids gather to watch the sunrise, marking the balance of light and dark. 
      Asian Celebrations
      • Japan (Shunbun no Hi): A national holiday for appreciating nature, family reunions, and visiting graves to honor ancestors. 
      • India & Nepal (Holi): A joyous festival of colors, music, and dancing, celebrating fertility, love, and the triumph of good over evil. 
      • Thailand (Songkran): The traditional Thai New Year, celebrated with massive water fights symbolizing purification and renewal. 
      Middle Eastern & Central Asian Traditions
      • Iran & Central Asia (Nowruz): The Persian New Year, a 3,000-year-old tradition symbolizing renewal, featuring fire jumping, feasts, and the symbolic Haft-Seen table. 
      • Zoroastrianism: Practices involve planting seeds and fire rituals for growth and purification. 
      European & Western Traditions
      • Pagan/Wiccan (Ostara): Celebrates fertility and new beginnings with symbols like eggs, rabbits, flowers, and bonfires. 
      • Switzerland (Sechseläuten): Burns a snowman figure (the Böögg) to welcome spring. 
      • Germany/Europe: Decorating trees with colored eggs (Ostereierbaum) echoes ancient fertility rites. 
      • Ireland (St. Patrick's Day): May have merged with older pagan equinox festivals, sharing themes of rebirth and nature. 
      Modern & General Rituals
      • Egg Games: Egg hunts, painting, and tapping games symbolize fertility and new life (common in Western cultures). 
      • Spring Altars: Setting up altars with flowers, candles, and natural objects to welcome the season.

        AI Overview
        Spring equinox traditions celebrate renewal with activities like egg decorating (Pysanky, Cascarónes), spring cleaning (Nowruz), planting seeds, having bonfires, and enjoying nature through activities like cherry blossom viewing or hiking, symbolizing fertility, new beginnings, and the balance of light and dark, as seen in pagan (Ostara), Persian (Nowruz), Indian (Holi), and Christian (Easter) celebrations.
         
        Global Celebrations
        • Nowruz (Persian New Year): Celebrated in Iran and neighboring countries with spring cleaning, jumping over fires for purification, and exchanging gifts, marking the New Year with the equinox. 
        • Holi (India/Nepal): A festival of colors where people throw colored powders and water, symbolizing the victory of good over evil and the arrival of spring. 
        • Cherry Blossom Festivals (Japan): Gatherings under blooming cherry trees (sakura) for food, drink, and appreciation of nature's transient beauty. 
        Pagan & Wiccan Traditions (Ostara)
        • Egg Decorating: Painting eggs (like Ukrainian Pysanky or German Ostereierbaum) to symbolize new life and fertility, a tradition predating Christianity. 
        • Planting Seeds: Ritualistically planting seeds as an act of intention-setting for growth and renewal. 
        • Altars & Candles: Creating altars with spring symbols (eggs, rabbits) and lighting candles to welcome returning warmth. 
        Other Traditions & Practices
        • Spring Cleaning: A widespread practice of decluttering homes to clear out the old and welcome fresh energy, linked to ancient equinox customs. 
        • Egg Balancing: An ancient Chinese custom of balancing eggs on their ends, believed to bring good luck (though possible any day). 
        • Outdoor Gatherings: Hiking, picnics, and communal meals to enjoy the warmer weather and nature's awakening. 
        • Bonfires: Lighting fires to release intentions and welcome the growing light.

          AI Overview
          The spring equinox marks the point when Earth's axis is tilted neither toward nor away from the Sun, causing day and night to be nearly equal in length globally, around 12 hours each, though slightly longer daylight occurs due to atmospheric refraction bending sunlight. It signals the start of astronomical spring, leading to days getting progressively longer, with the rate of daylight increase peaking around the equinox.
           
          What Happens on the Equinox:
          • Sun's Position:
            The Sun shines directly over the equator, crossing from the Southern Hemisphere into the Northern Hemisphere. 
          • Equal Day & Night:
            The term "equinox" means "equal night" in Latin, reflecting the near-equal hours of daylight and darkness everywhere on Earth. 
          Why Days Aren't Exactly 12 Hours: 
          • Atmospheric Refraction:
            Earth's atmosphere bends sunlight, making the Sun appear to rise earlier and set later than it geometrically would, adding several minutes of extra daylight.
          • Definition of Day:
            Daylight is defined as the time from the first glimpse of the Sun's upper edge to the last glimpse, which is extended by refraction.
          Post-Equinox Effect: 
          • Increasing Daylight: After the spring equinox, days become longer than nights, and the rate at which daylight increases (minutes per day) is at its fastest, continuing until the summer solstice.

            AI Overview
            The spring equinox signifies rebirth, renewal, and balance, marking the astronomical start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere with nearly equal day and night, representing nature awakening after winter, fertility, new beginnings, and often seen as a spiritual reset or the start of the zodiac year (Aries season). It's celebrated across cultures with rituals for growth, new intentions, and the triumph of light over darkness. 
            Astronomical Significance
            • Equal Day & Night: The Earth's axis is tilted neither toward nor away from the Sun, resulting in roughly 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of darkness. 
            • Start of Seasons: It marks the beginning of spring in the Northern Hemisphere and autumn in the Southern Hemisphere. 
            Cultural & Spiritual Significance
            • Renewal & Rebirth: A powerful symbol of life bursting forth, mirroring nature's awakening from winter dormancy. 
            • Fertility & Abundance: Associated with the Earth's fertility and the promise of a bountiful year. 
            • Balance: Represents a dynamic balance between light and dark, the feminine and masculine energies. 
            • New Beginnings: A time for setting intentions, personal transformation, and embarking on new journeys. 
            Examples of Celebrations
            • Astrology: The start of Aries season and the astrological new year. 
            • Ancient Sites: The Mayan pyramid at Chichen Itza shows a serpent shadow descending the steps. 
            • Festivals: Celebrated in traditions like Nowruz (Persian New Year), Holi, and ancient Celtic festivals. 
            • Modern Practices: Rituals, meditation, and connecting with nature to harness the energy of change.

              AI Overview
              The spring equinox marks the astronomical start of spring in the Northern Hemisphere, signaling longer days and increasing sunlight as the Earth tilts toward the sun, leading to warmer temperatures, but actual warmth lags due to the Earth's thermal inertia (thermal lag) from winter, often bringing cool, wet, or stormy conditions (like atmospheric rivers) as warmer air mixes with lingering cold, creating significant weather shifts. 
              How it influences weather:
              • More Sunlight, More Heat: The primary effect is the gradual increase in daylight hours and the sun's angle, delivering more direct solar energy, which drives warming trends. 
              • Thermal Lag: Despite more sun, spring equinox days aren't the warmest because oceans and land retain winter's cold; it takes time to heat up. This is why spring often feels cooler than late May, even with equal day/night hours.
              • Transitional Weather: This period is famous for "weather whiplash" – rapid shifts from cold, even snowy, conditions to warmer spells, often fueled by powerful storms (like atmospheric rivers) as contrasting air masses collide. 
              • Equal Day/Night: The equinox means roughly equal hours of day and night globally, but for the Northern Hemisphere, it's the start of days being longer than nights, while the Southern Hemisphere experiences its autumn equinox (shorter days). 
              • Biological Triggers: The warming trend and longer days trigger plant growth (budding, blooming) and animal activity (waking from hibernation, migration), marking the seasonal shift. 
              In essence, the spring equinox is the start of the warming trend, but the actual feeling of spring warmth arrives gradually as the atmosphere adjusts, often with dramatic, unsettled weather.

The Spring Equinox is the second of the spring festivals, a time where we can really notice the quickening of the natural world. The sun rises at its most easterly position and sets at its most westerly during the Equinox, creating an equal balance of day and night. Some view this as a balance of masculine and feminine, important symbols during the stirrings of fertility in nature. Fertility rituals and rites played a large role in this festival, with symbols such as hares, eggs, and seeds used in ceremony and celebration.
